narrative:
The 2026 New York Mets entered the season with genuine aspirations, bolstered by the additions of Luis Robert Jr. and a revamped rotation. But the campaign was derailed almost immediately by a catastrophic April, a 7-19 month that buried them in the standings before spring had even settled in. The bullpen was a recurring problem, with Devin Williams and Austin Warren each surrendering crushing blows at the worst possible moments, and the starting staff struggled to provide consistent length. By the time May arrived, the Mets were already playing from a significant deficit.

May brought the first real sign of life, a 16-12 record that stood as the best month of the season. Tyrone Taylor's three-run blast on May 17th was the kind of moment that suggested the lineup could still punish mistakes, and the rotation stabilized enough to string together winning stretches. June undid much of that goodwill, however, another losing month dragged down by a shaky pen and a pair of demoralizing home runs surrendered by Kodai Senga and Austin Warren. The Mets were treading water at best.

July became the most emotionally complex chapter of the season. Juan Soto delivered the single highest-leverage swing of the year, a go-ahead three-run homer on July 6th, and Luis Torrens followed later that same dramatic afternoon with a two-run double that kept the Mets alive. The month also brought Tyrone Taylor's eighth homer and a Luis Robert Jr. single that plated two runs in a July 30th win. Yet the Mets still finished July at 11-14, unable to sustain the momentum those individual moments generated. August was healthier, a 15-12 mark, anchored by Francisco Alvarez stepping up and Bo Bichette emerging as a clutch presence down the stretch.

September has seen the Mets play even baseball at 12-12 through the games captured here, a cruel kind of competence that arrived too late to matter in the standings. A season-long record of 74-88 tells the story plainly: the April collapse was simply too deep a hole to climb out of. The offense generated moments of real beauty — 204 home runs, a lineup capable of explosive innings — but the pitching staff allowed 32 more runs than it prevented, and a bullpen that surrendered games in nearly every critical moment proved to be the season's defining flaw. This was a Mets team that showed flashes of what it could be, surrounded by far too many reminders of what it still isn't.

chapters.title: Opening Day Promise, April Disaster
chapters.description: A Luis Robert Jr. home run sparks early optimism, but the Mets collapse through April in historic fashion, going 7-19 amid a parade of bullpen catastrophes.

chapters.title: May Revival
chapters.description: Tyrone Taylor's three-run blast leads a 16-12 month that represents the Mets' best baseball of the season and briefly reignites hope.

chapters.title: June Fade
chapters.description: The rotation falters again and the bullpen surrenders late leads, sending the Mets back below .500 for the summer.

chapters.title: Soto and the July Rollercoaster
chapters.description: Juan Soto delivers the most electrifying swing of the season and the Mets produce multiple clutch moments, yet still finish July 11-14 and unable to climb out.

chapters.title: August Resurgence
chapters.description: Francisco Alvarez steps up and the Mets go 15-12, their second-best month, with bright individual performances masking the irreversible standings damage.

chapters.title: September's Too-Late Lessons
chapters.description: Bo Bichette and A.J. Ewing deliver memorable moments in a 12-12 September, a competent but ultimately hollow finish to a season defined by April's wreckage.
